sections.text: Introduction: Your Medicare Coverage May Hold a Few Surprises

sections.content: Enrolling in Medicare feels like crossing a finish line, but the details keep evolving long after your card arrives. Many people discover gaps in their coverage only after a bill shows up that they didn't expect. Costs shift, provider networks change, and deadlines carry consequences that last for years.

This article walks through five lesser-known facts about Medicare coverage in 2026 that can affect your budget and your care. Each one connects to a common worry, from unexpected expenses to fear of losing a trusted doctor. Understanding these details now can help you avoid surprises later and feel more settled in your choices.

sections.text: 1. Original Medicare Doesn't Cover Everything You Might Assume

sections.content: Part A and Part B cover a wide range of hospital and medical services, but the gaps catch many people off guard. Routine dental care, most vision exams and glasses, and hearing aids are generally not included. Long-term custodial care, like help with daily activities in a nursing home, also falls outside Original Medicare's coverage.

This is part of why comparing plan types can feel overwhelming. [Medicare Advantage plans](/faqs/medicare-advantage-vs-medicare-supplement/) often include some of these extra benefits, while Original Medicare paired with a standalone dental or vision policy is another route entirely. Without knowing what's excluded, it's easy to assume you're protected when you're not.

sections.calloutText: Someone enrolled only in Original Medicare might need a full set of dentures and discover the entire cost falls to them, since routine dental work isn't a covered benefit under Part A or Part B.

sections.content: Knowing these exclusions ahead of time helps you decide whether additional coverage makes sense for your health needs. It also explains why so many people compare Medicare Advantage and Medigap options before settling on a plan. The right choice depends on your personal health history and the services you expect to use.

sections.text: 2. Your Costs Can Change Even If You Keep the Same Plan

sections.content: Keeping the same plan year after year doesn't mean your costs stay the same. Premiums, deductibles, and copays are reviewed and often adjusted annually, even without you making a single change. In 2026, the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month, up from $185 in 2025, and the Part B deductible has risen to $283.

sections.content: Out-of-pocket costs for a Medicare Advantage or Part D plan can shift too, sometimes significantly, even if the plan name and network look identical. Every fall, plans send an [Annual Notice of Change letter](/faqs/medicare-annual-notice-of-change-letter/) explaining what's different for the coming year. Skimming past this letter is one of the most common ways people get caught off guard by new costs.

sections.calloutText: The Annual Notice of Change letter outlines premium, deductible, and formulary updates for your plan. Reading it each fall is the simplest way to avoid a surprise increase in January.

sections.content: Reviewing your coverage every year, rather than assuming nothing has changed, gives you the chance to catch cost increases before they hit your budget. It also opens the door to comparing other plans if your current one no longer fits your needs.

sections.text: 3. Your Doctors and Prescriptions May Not Always Be Covered the Way You Expect

sections.content: Provider networks and drug formularies aren't fixed. A doctor who was in-network last year might leave a plan's network for the next, and a medication that was covered at a low tier could move to a higher, more expensive tier. These shifts happen quietly and often go unnoticed until you're at the pharmacy counter or scheduling an appointment.

This is one of the most common fears people carry into their Medicare decisions: losing access to a trusted physician or facing a sudden cost spike for a needed medication. The good news is that this risk is manageable with a little preparation.

items: Check the plan's provider directory each year to confirm your doctors and specialists remain in-network
Review the plan's drug formulary to see if your prescriptions are covered and at what tier
Call your doctor's office directly to confirm they still accept the plan, since directories aren't always current
Compare formulary tiers across plans if a medication's cost has increased significantly

sections.content: Taking these steps before you need care, rather than after, keeps your coverage aligned with your actual healthcare needs. It also reduces the chance of an unpleasant surprise mid-year when switching plans isn't as simple.

I always tell people to check their plan's provider directory and formulary every single year, even if they love their current coverage. I've seen too many clients assume nothing changed, only to find their go-to specialist left the network or their medication jumped a tier. A ten-minute check each fall can save you months of frustration.

sections.text: 4. Missing Certain Deadlines Can Lead to Lasting Penalties

sections.content: Medicare's enrollment windows aren't just formalities. Missing them can mean paying a penalty that follows you for as long as you have coverage. If you delay Part B enrollment without qualifying employer coverage, your premium can increase by 10% for each 12-month period you were eligible but didn't enroll.

Part D carries its own penalty, calculated using the national base beneficiary premium and added to your monthly premium for as long as you're enrolled. For 2026, that base premium is $38.99, and even a short lapse in creditable drug coverage can trigger a lasting cost.

sections.calloutText: Late enrollment penalties for Part B and Part D aren't one-time fees. They're added to your premium permanently, which is why understanding your enrollment window matters as much as choosing a plan.

sections.content: Confusion often arises around delaying enrollment while still working, since employer coverage can sometimes qualify you for a Special Enrollment Period later. But the rules depend on the size of your employer and the type of coverage you have, so it's worth confirming your specific situation rather than assuming you're covered.

Marking your Initial Enrollment Period and any Special Enrollment Period on a calendar, well before the deadline arrives, is one of the simplest ways to avoid this entirely. Waiting until the last minute leaves little room to fix a mistake.

sections.text: 5. You're Allowed to Compare and Change Plans More Often Than You Might Think

sections.content: A common misconception is that choosing a Medicare plan locks you in for good. In reality, you have regular opportunities to review and switch coverage. The Annual Enrollment Period, running from October 15 to December 7 each year, lets you change Medicare Advantage or Part D plans for the following year.

There's also the [Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/), from January 1 to March 31, which allows those already enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan to switch to a different Medicare Advantage plan or return to Original Medicare.

Switch Medicare Advantage plans or return to Original Medicare
Make changes outside standard windows due to life events

sections.content: If your current plan no longer covers your doctors well, or your prescription costs have climbed, you're not stuck. Reviewing your coverage each year is a normal part of managing Medicare, not a sign that you chose incorrectly the first time.

sections.calloutText: Your health needs and budget can shift year to year, and your Medicare coverage is built to allow for that. Comparing plans annually is a routine check-in, not an admission of a past mistake.

sections.text: How to Make Sense of These Details Without Feeling Overwhelmed

sections.content: A practical way to approach all of this is to start with a simple list before comparing anything. Write down your current doctors, your medications, and a realistic monthly budget. This gives you a clear reference point instead of trying to weigh dozens of plan features at once.

Once you have that list, comparing coverage becomes a matter of checking a plan against your specific needs, rather than guessing which one sounds best. This approach cuts down on decision fatigue and helps you focus on what actually matters for your health and finances.

Licensed Medicare agents can also walk through these details with you, answering questions about networks, formularies, and costs without any pressure to enroll immediately. Their role is to explain your options clearly, so you can make a decision on your own timeline.
Asking questions now, before a deadline or a plan change forces your hand, is one of the most effective ways to prevent regret and unexpected costs down the road.

sections.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Understanding Your Medicare Coverage

faqs.question: I want to review my coverage, but I'm not ready to talk to anyone yet. Is that okay?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking time to read and research on your own first is a completely reasonable step. Resources like MedicareFAQ are available whenever you're ready, whether that's today or a few months from now, with no pressure to act sooner.

faqs.question: Will reaching out for help lead to constant sales calls?
faqs.answer: Licensed agents are meant to answer your questions and explain your options, not push you toward a decision. Reputable sources are transparent about how communication works and respect your timeline, so you can ask questions without worrying about being pressured.

faqs.question: Can I figure out these details on my own by reading more?
faqs.answer: Self-research is valuable, and many people learn a great deal by reading articles like this one. Personal guidance becomes especially helpful for specific tasks, like confirming a doctor's network status or checking whether a medication is covered on a plan's formulary.

faqs.question: How do I know which sources about Medicare coverage I can trust?
faqs.answer: Look for plain-language explanations, licensed agents who explain rather than sell, and a clear plan comparison process built around your doctors, prescriptions, and budget. Reviewing client testimonials or reviews before making a decision is another good way to gauge trustworthiness.

sections.text: Conclusion: Feel Confident, Not Confused, About Your Coverage

sections.content: Medicare coverage involves more nuance than most people expect, from gaps in Original Medicare to shifting costs, network changes, enrollment deadlines, and the freedom to switch plans when needed. Each of these five details plays a role in how much you pay and how well your care is covered.

Reviewing your coverage regularly, rather than assuming it stays the same, helps you sidestep penalties and unwelcome surprises. Comparing plans based on your doctors, prescriptions, and budget puts you in a stronger position to choose coverage that actually fits your life.
When you're ready to talk through your options, clear and no-pressure guidance is available to help you compare plans with confidence.
